questions.q: Alice asks Bob for his public key over an insecure channel and encrypts her message under whatever key comes back. What can an active attacker, Mallory, do?
choices: Nothing useful: without Bob's private key, Mallory cannot read the message
Swap in her own public key, decrypt Alice's ciphertext, then re-encrypt the message (possibly altered) under Bob's real key so neither side notices
Only read the message. Any change would be detected because Bob could no longer decrypt it
Recover Bob's private key from his public key while it is in transit
questions.explain: Mallory replaces Bob's key with her own. Alice encrypts to Mallory, who decrypts, reads or changes the message, and re-encrypts it under Bob's real public key. No cryptography is broken. The flaw is that Alice could not authenticate the key.

questions.q: In a man-in-the-middle attack on a public-key exchange, Bob will always notice the attack because he receives ciphertext he cannot decrypt with his private key.
questions.explain: Mallory re-encrypts the message, possibly modified, under Bob's real public key before forwarding it, so Bob decrypts it normally and suspects nothing.

questions.q: What is the root cause that makes the naive 'just send me your public key' exchange vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack?
choices: The channel lacks a shared symmetric key
Bob's private key travels over the network
The public-key encryption scheme is too weak
Alice has no way to verify that the public key she received really belongs to Bob
questions.explain: MITM works because Alice cannot authenticate Bob's claimed public key. The general defense is to make sure every participant can verify that other people's public keys are authentic.

questions.q: Alice and Bob send their public keys to each other over an insecure channel, and Mallory sits between them. What can Mallory achieve?
choices: Read the messages Alice sends to Bob
Read the messages Bob sends to Alice
Alter messages in either direction without either party noticing
Learn Alice's and Bob's private keys
questions.explain: Mallory runs the key-substitution attack in both directions, so she can read and alter all traffic. She never learns their private keys, and she doesn't need them.

questions.q: An attacker who places himself between two parties and reads, relays, and possibly alters their traffic while both think they are talking directly to each other is mounting what kind of attack?
questions.explain: This is a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack. The attacker sits between the two parties.

questions.q: Alice gets Bob's public key from a trusted directory, Dirk, over an insecure network. What keeps an attacker from tampering with Dirk's reply?
choices: Nothing can; a directory service is always open to MITM
Dirk includes his own public key in every reply
Alice authenticates Dirk's reply using Dirk's public key, which is hardcoded into her application
Alice asks Bob to confirm the key over the same insecure channel
questions.explain: Alice needs Dirk's public key to authenticate his replies, and that key can be hardcoded into the software. If Dirk's key arrived with each reply, an attacker could just replace it.

questions.q: Which of these are shortcomings of a trusted directory service for public keys?
choices: Everyone's security depends on the directory operating correctly and honestly
It becomes a bottleneck, since everyone must contact it before talking to someone new
It is a single point of failure and a global denial-of-service target
Users cannot look up keys while offline
Its servers must be Internet-connected at all times, so they must be hardened against remote attacks
It can never be protected from MITM, because its own public key cannot be distributed safely
questions.explain: Trust, scalability, reliability, the online requirement, and server security are all real drawbacks. The last choice is false: hardcoding the directory's public key into applications solves that problem.

questions.q: Alice is on a flight with no Internet. She wants to encrypt an email to Bob, whose key she has never looked up. Which directory-service limitation is she running into?
choices: Trust
Scalability
Security of the directory's servers
The need to be online
questions.explain: A directory has to be queried in real time, so a disconnected user can't look up a new key.

questions.q: Why is a central key directory a reasonable choice for a messenger such as Signal, despite the usual drawbacks?
choices: Sending a message already requires being online, so needing the directory online costs little
Messengers use only symmetric keys, so no public keys are looked up
Signal's directory is run by a CA that every browser trusts
Messenger users never contact anyone new
questions.explain: The directory's biggest practical drawback is that it must be online. In a messenger, Alice already has to be online to send anything.

questions.q: Under 'trust but verify' (key transparency), Alice and Bob get each other's keys from a central keyserver and later compare them on their devices when they meet in person. What does this achieve?
choices: It removes the need for the keyserver entirely
It upgrades their future messages to a stronger key
It acts as a check on the keyserver: a rogue keyserver that hands out false keys knows it might get caught
It revokes any key the keyserver issued by mistake
questions.explain: The in-person comparison is inconvenient, but it means a rogue keyserver always risks being caught, and that discourages misbehavior.

questions.q: What is a digital certificate?
choices: An encrypted copy of a person's private key held by a trusted party
A list of public keys kept on an online directory server
A statement linking a name to a public key, digitally signed by a certifying party
A symmetric key shared between a user and a CA
questions.explain: A certificate records a claimed link between a person's name and their public key, and a certifying party vouches for it with a signature. It is just data and can be shared freely.

questions.q: In the notation {M}_{SK^-1}, what does the expression denote?
choices: M encrypted under the public key SK
A MAC on M computed with the shared key SK
M decrypted with the inverse of SK
A digital signature on M made with the private key SK^-1
questions.explain: {M}_{SK^-1} is a signature on M made with the private key SK^-1. A certificate is a statement such as 'David's public key is K' written in this signed form.

questions.q: It is unsafe for Alice to download David's certificate from an untrusted website over an insecure channel.
questions.explain: A certificate validates itself. If Alice checks the signature with a correct copy of the signer's public key and trusts the signer, it doesn't matter where the certificate came from. Any tampering would make the signature fail.

questions.q: Alice has a certificate, signed by Jerry, that states David's public key. What does she need before she can rely on that key?
choices: A correct copy of Jerry's public key
A successful check of the certificate's signature using Jerry's public key
Trust that Jerry is honest and careful about verifying identities before he signs
A copy of the certificate obtained directly from David over a secure channel
An online connection to Jerry at the moment she checks the certificate
questions.explain: Alice builds her trust in David's key from three things: a correct copy of Jerry's key, a valid signature, and her belief that Jerry signs only statements he has checked. She can get the certificate from anywhere and can verify it offline.

questions.q: On its own, a valid signature by Jerry on 'David's public key is K' proves what?
choices: That Jerry chose to sign that statement with his private key
That K definitely belongs to David
That David created the certificate himself
That no one else has ever seen K
questions.explain: The signature proves that Jerry agreed to the statement. Whether the statement is true depends on Jerry's honesty and competence, which is why Alice must also trust Jerry.

questions.q: Which limitations of a trusted directory service do digital certificates help with?
choices: Scalability
Reliability (a single central point of failure)
Needing to be online to look up a key
Needing complete trust in a central party
questions.explain: A certificate can be obtained from anyone and checked offline, so no central server has to answer every request. The certificate's issuer still has to be trusted, so the trust problem remains.

questions.q: How does a web browser normally know which public keys to use when checking a CA's signature on a site's certificate?
choices: It downloads them from the website being visited
It asks the user to type them in
It queries an online directory on every visit
It ships with a built-in list of trusted CAs and their public keys
questions.explain: Every browser ships with a list of trusted CAs. Their public keys are effectively hardcoded, which starts the chain of trust.

questions.q: When you visit an https: URL, which steps does the browser take before it trusts the site's public key?
choices: Get a copy of the site's certificate
Check the certificate's signature using the public key of the CA that issued it
Check that the domain name in the certificate matches the site you asked to visit
Contact the CA live to ask whether the site is legitimate
Ask the site to send its private key for comparison
questions.explain: The browser gets the certificate, checks the CA's signature, confirms the domain name matches, and then uses the certificate's public key. It never contacts the CA live, and it never sees the site's private key.

questions.q: Mallory owns mallory.com and has a valid CA-signed certificate for it. If a browser skipped the check that the certificate's domain name matches the requested site, what could Mallory do?
choices: Nothing, because her certificate is signed by a trusted CA
Present her mallory.com certificate while posing as another site, such as bank.com, in a man-in-the-middle attack
Forge signatures from the CA
Revoke bank.com's certificate
questions.explain: A valid signature only proves which key goes with which name. Without the name check, any valid certificate would be accepted for any site.

questions.q: If a browser trusts 88 CAs, it accepts a certificate for amazon.com only when the certificate comes from the CA that Amazon chose to buy from.
questions.explain: The browser accepts any certificate from any of its trusted CAs. If any one of the 88 issues an amazon.com certificate, the browser accepts it.

questions.q: Why does trusting more CAs increase the risk of a security breach?
choices: If any single trusted CA issues a certificate to the wrong party, or acts maliciously, every site's users can be affected
Each extra CA slows down signature checking
More CAs mean more certificate chains that must all verify
CAs share their private keys with each other
questions.explain: A browser trusts every CA on its list equally for every domain, so overall security is only as strong as the weakest CA on that list.

questions.q: Which drawback of a trusted directory service still applies when you rely on a CA?
choices: The CA must be online for every lookup
The CA is a bottleneck that has to answer every new connection
Everyone's security depends on the CA behaving honestly and carefully
Users cannot get keys while offline
questions.explain: Certificates fix the scalability, reliability, and online problems. The CA must still be trusted, and if it is malicious or careless, users' security can be breached.

questions.q: What is a certificate chain?
choices: A list of certificates that a CA has revoked
Several certificates for the same person issued by different CAs
A single certificate signed by several CAs
A sequence of certificates, each of which authenticates the public key of the party who signs the next one
questions.explain: Each link vouches for the key of the next signer, so trust in the root key extends down to the final certificate.

questions.q: Alice knows only Jerry's public key. She receives (1) {UC's public key is PK_N} signed with Jerry's private key, and (2) {David's public key is PK_daw} signed with Napolitano's private key. How does she get David's key?
choices: Check (2) with Jerry's public key, then check (1) with PK_daw
Check (1) with Jerry's public key to learn PK_N, then check (2) with PK_N
Check (2) with PK_daw itself, because David's certificate vouches for itself
She can't, because she would need Napolitano's key in advance
questions.explain: She starts from the key she trusts (Jerry's) and checks the first certificate, which gives her Napolitano's key. She then uses that key to check David's certificate.

questions.q: A root CA certifies a country CA, which certifies a state CA, which certifies a city CA, which certifies Alice's public key. How many certificates are in the chain from the root down to Alice's key?
questions.explain: There are four certificates: root to country, country to state, state to city, and city to Alice.

questions.q: What is the main reason to use a hierarchy of CAs instead of one CA that signs everyone's certificate?
choices: Scalability: one party can't personally verify hundreds of thousands of people, so it hands the authority to sign down to others
Each extra level makes signatures harder to forge
It removes the need to trust the root CA
It makes certificates shorter
questions.explain: A single signer can't check everyone's identity. Each level delegates (and may sub-delegate) the power to issue certificates for its part of the organization.

questions.q: Which statements about hierarchical PKI are true?
choices: The hierarchy forms a tree
Certificate chains can be of any length
The CA hierarchy often follows an organization's structure
Every certificate must be signed directly by the root CA
questions.explain: The hierarchy is a tree of any depth and usually follows the organization's structure. Only the top-level certificates are signed by the root.

questions.q: In the chain Jerry -> Napolitano -> David, Jerry checks identities perfectly, but Napolitano carelessly certifies an impostor's key as David's. Alice, who trusts only Jerry's key, could still be fooled.
questions.explain: Jerry's certificate gives Napolitano authority to vouch for UC employees. Relying on a chain means relying on every signer in it.

questions.q: In the basic certificate scheme, with no expiration dates and no revocation lists, a CA has no way to cancel a certificate it issued by mistake.
questions.explain: Without a revocation mechanism, a certificate stays valid forever once it is issued.

questions.q: Verisign issued bogus 'Microsoft Corporation' certificates to someone other than Microsoft. How was the problem finally fixed?
choices: Verisign added them to its revocation list
The certificates expired the next day
Microsoft shipped a Windows patch that contained the bogus certificates and treated them as invalid
Browsers removed Verisign from their trusted CA lists
questions.explain: Verisign had no way to revoke the certificates. The patch worked only because Microsoft could push software to affected machines, a fix that wouldn't exist for a bogus certificate for an ordinary website.

questions.q: A CA issues certificates that are valid for only one day. What is the main cost of this approach?
choices: Bad certificates stay valid for years
Certificates can no longer be checked offline
Revocation lists grow very large
Legitimate parties must contact the CA constantly, which adds load and causes reliability problems when the CA is unreachable
questions.explain: Short lifetimes let a bad certificate be dealt with quickly, since it is simply not reissued. The cost is heavy load and dependence on the CA. Long lifetimes reverse this tradeoff.

questions.q: Validity periods let a CA revoke a bad certificate the moment it discovers the mistake.
questions.explain: An expiration date only limits the damage: the bad certificate keeps working until it expires.

questions.q: Clients that can't download a fresh revocation list keep using their old copy. How can an attacker holding a bogus certificate exploit this?
choices: Launch a DoS attack on the CA's revocation servers so clients never learn that the certificate was revoked
Forge an entry on the signed revocation list
Keep using the certificate after it expires
Nothing, because the old list already contains the revocation
questions.explain: If the revocation happened after the client's last download, blocking the servers keeps the bogus certificate accepted.

questions.q: Suppose clients instead reject every certificate whenever they can't get a fresh revocation list. What is the danger?
choices: Bogus certificates get accepted
A sustained DoS attack on the CA's revocation servers can deny service to every user of the network
The CA's private key is exposed
Revocation lists can no longer be signed
questions.explain: This fails safe, but it gives an attacker an even worse DoS: knocking out the revocation servers breaks every certificate check.

questions.q: When can revocation lists be more efficient than constantly reissuing certificates with short validity periods?
choices: When certificates are revoked constantly
When clients are never online
When revocation is rare, so the list stays short
When the CA has no private key
questions.explain: A short list is cheap to download and check, so it beats reissuing every certificate. Clients still pay a cost that grows with how often they download it.

questions.q: Why should a CA date and digitally sign its revocation list?
choices: To encrypt the revoked certificates
So clients can confirm the list really came from the CA and see how recent it is
To make the list smaller
So revoked certificates can be restored later
questions.explain: Clients download the list over ordinary channels. The signature proves it is authentic, and the date shows how fresh it is.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the web of trust, pioneered by PGP?
choices: One global CA signs everyone's key
Keys are accepted on first use and remembered
Anyone can issue certificates for people they know, so key verification doesn't depend on a single central authority
A central directory answers key lookups in real time
questions.explain: The web of trust spreads out certification: people sign keys for friends and colleagues, and chains of these signatures connect strangers.

questions.q: Alice trusts Bob. Bob signed Carol's key after carefully checking her ID. Carol signed a key labeled 'Doug'. Why might Alice be wrong to trust that key?
choices: Bob's signature can't be checked
Bob's signature vouches for Carol's identity, not for her honesty or care when she signs other people's keys
PGP doesn't allow chains longer than one
Carol's key is too old
questions.explain: If Carol is sloppy or malicious, she might certify an impostor's key as Doug's, and Bob's careful ID check of Carol does nothing to prevent that.

questions.q: 'Alice trusts Bob not to deliberately deceive her, but doubts that he checks IDs carefully before signing keys.' Which challenge does this illustrate?
choices: Trust isn't transitive
Key continuity
Trust isn't absolute
Single point of failure
questions.explain: We trust people for specific purposes. Trusting Bob's intentions is different from trusting how diligent he is, or his judgment about third parties.

questions.q: 'Alice considers Bob trustworthy, and Bob considers Carol trustworthy, but Alice does not consider Carol trustworthy.' Which challenge does this illustrate?
choices: Trust isn't transitive
Trust isn't absolute
Single point of failure
Leap of faith
questions.explain: Alice trusting Bob and Bob trusting Carol does not mean Alice trusts Carol.

questions.q: How does PGP try to increase confidence in a key it finds through the web of trust?
choices: It requires every key to be signed by a root CA
It sets a one-day validity period on every key
It asks the recipient to sign their own key
It looks for multiple paths to the recipient, treating more and shorter paths as more trustworthy
questions.explain: It's unclear whether this heuristic has a principled basis or actually solves the transitivity and absoluteness problems.

questions.q: Which of these are criticisms of the web of trust?
choices: Many users find it hard to understand
Usability hurdles, such as poor integration with mainstream mail readers
It doesn't capture that trust is neither transitive nor absolute
It depends on one central authority that everyone must trust
Keys can only be looked up while online
questions.explain: The web of trust has no central authority by design. Its problems are usability and a poor model of how people actually trust each other.

questions.q: What does an SSH client do the first time it connects to a server it has never seen?
choices: Checks the server's certificate against a list of trusted CAs
Looks up the server's key in a trusted directory
Accepts whatever public key the server sends, remembers it, and uses it on later connections
Refuses to connect until the user types in the server's key
questions.explain: The server sends its key unprotected, and the client simply accepts it, usually after the user clicks OK. Later connections reuse the remembered key.

questions.q: Leap-of-faith authentication is also known by the acronym TOFU. What does TOFU stand for?
questions.explain: Trust On First Use: the client trusts the key on its first connection and expects that same key afterward.

questions.q: Leap-of-faith authentication tries to make sure that a server's public key stays the same over a long period, so it is also called key ______ management. Fill in the blank.
questions.explain: It's called key continuity management because the key tied to a server is expected to stay the same over time.

questions.q: Which attackers does leap-of-faith authentication protect against?
choices: A passive eavesdropper
An active attacker who was not present during the first connection
An active man-in-the-middle during the very first connection
questions.explain: It is weak only on the first connection. An attacker who intercepts that one can substitute his own key. Otherwise it stops eavesdropping and any attacker who arrives later.

questions.q: You SSH into a server you have used many times, and it now presents a different public key from the one your client remembered. Under key continuity, why is this a warning sign?
choices: The server's key is supposed to stay the same over time, so a change may mean someone in the middle is presenting their own key
SSH keys expire daily, so a change is expected
It means a CA revoked the server's certificate
It means your own private key was stolen
questions.explain: Key continuity relies on the remembered key staying the same. A different key breaks that and is exactly what a later MITM attacker would cause.

questions.q: Which usable-security principle says users shouldn't need to configure their software or take an explicit step to turn security on?
choices: Trust isn't transitive
Least privilege
Defense in depth
There should be only one mode of operation, and it should be secure
questions.explain: Security should always be on and automatic in every case, as it is in SSH's key continuity.

questions.q: Why might a well-designed system not let users switch its security protections off at all?
choices: Switching them off would slow the system down
It opens the door to social engineering, where an attacker talks the user into disabling the cryptography
Users would need to understand cryptography to switch them back on
Security settings can't be stored
questions.explain: If security can be turned off, an attacker can try to persuade the user to turn it off.

questions.q: A sound usable-security principle is that users shouldn't have to understand cryptography to use a system securely, though the system's designers should.
questions.explain: It is reasonable to expect designers to understand cryptography, but not users. SSH's leap-of-faith approach hides the key management from the user.

questions.q: Which key-management approach requires contacting a separate trusted party in real time every time you start talking to someone new?
choices: Digital certificates issued by a CA
Trusted directory service
Leap-of-faith authentication
Web of trust
questions.explain: A directory must be asked for every new contact. A certificate can be fetched from anywhere and checked offline.

questions.q: Which of these approaches does NOT rely on a single central trusted authority?
choices: Trusted directory service
Hierarchical PKI with one root CA
Web of trust
The browser CA model
questions.explain: The web of trust deliberately spreads certification across ordinary users. The other three all depend on a central authority or a fixed set of them.

questions.q: Which approach lets Alice get Bob's key from any untrusted source (a search result, a whiteboard, Bob himself) and still verify it while offline?
choices: Digital certificates
Trusted directory service
Leap-of-faith authentication
Asking Bob for his key over the insecure channel
questions.explain: A certificate validates itself: the trusted signer's signature can be checked offline no matter where the certificate came from.
